evals.prompt: We're Flagstone - hosted feature-flag evaluation, 210 paying teams on $19/user/month. Seat count per account has been flat at 5.4 for fourteen months while flag evaluations went from 40M to 380M a month. Revenue is basically flat. Everyone on the team is saying go usage-based. Problem: we can read seats, projects and environments straight off our account records today, but metering evaluations per account is a solid quarter of backend work and it is not in this year's budget. What should we do about the pricing model?
evals.expected_output: A metric diagnosis naming the seat collapse, an explicit brainstorm across all metric families, consumption deleted rather than demoted because nothing is meterable and no engineering is funded, capacity or entitlement promoted for the near term, an additive repair rather than a wholesale swap, and two or three candidate architectures with a recommendation.
expectations: Identifies the seat-collapse pattern, citing the flat 5.4 seats per account against the 40M to 380M evaluation growth as the diagnostic evidence
Deletes consumption from the candidate list outright rather than ranking it last, on the grounds that nothing is meterable today and no billing engineering is funded
Promotes capacity or entitlement - environments, projects or concurrency - as the near-term metric because it bills off account state the product already stores
Treats the metric repair as additive: keeps a seat component for the human console surface and adds a second layer for the automated load
Warns that a wholesale metric swap re-prices every existing account at once and turns a metric fix into a churn event
States explicitly that it is entering brainstorming mode before widening the candidate list

Lists candidates from every metric family - seats, consumption, business outcome, capacity or entitlement, percentage of a flow, flat per unit of software - and marks each plausible, unmeterable today, or misaligned with the reason

Puts surviving candidates through five tests in writing: moves with value, already counted by the customer, forecastable before the invoice, not gameable or perverse, and correlated with cost to serve
States the efficiency ranking of the metric families out loud rather than leaving it implied by the order of the list
Presents two or three candidate pricing architectures, never a single one, and recommends among them
For each candidate architecture, gives the unit, what a typical customer's bill looks like, what it gives up, and how it behaves when the customer succeeds
Treats a hybrid - platform fee, included allowance, metered overage, optional committed spend - as a first-class candidate rather than a compromise
Notes that changing a live value metric rewrites every contract, every forecast and the metering pipeline underneath, unlike packaging or price points which can be re-cut in a quarter
Does not recommend moving all 210 existing accounts onto a new metric on a single date

evals.prompt: Kestrelbase is our Apache-2.0 time-series database - roughly 1,400 known self-hosted deployments. We're launching Kestrelbase Cloud next quarter. Marginal cost is $0.0009 per million points ingested plus $0.011 per GB-month stored, and our heaviest 10% of beta accounts cost about 4x the median account. A mid-sized team self-hosting spends roughly $260/month on infrastructure and about 5 engineer-hours a month keeping it alive. The nearest managed competitor lists $400/month flat. What should Cloud cost?
evals.expected_output: A floor computed from marginal cost at the 90th-percentile account with the free surface carried inside it, a self-host ceiling quantified in the customer's terms including operator time, the competitor price used only as a bound, and a margin target chosen deliberately against the usage-pricing median.
expectations: Computes the floor from marginal cost plus a gross-margin target rather than from the $400 competitor price
Models the floor on the 90th-percentile account - the heaviest decile costing about 4x the median - rather than on the average or median account
Labels the 90th-percentile modelling choice as this skill's own baseline rather than an industry benchmark
Carries the free surface's total marginal cost as a line item inside the margin calculation rather than outside it
Identifies self-hosting as the binding ceiling for a product with a free self-hostable equivalent
Computes the self-host ceiling as infrastructure plus operator time plus upgrade risk plus on-call, quantified in the customer's terms rather than the vendor's
Converts the 5 engineer-hours a month into a loaded cost figure and adds it to the $260 infrastructure cost
Treats the $400 competitor price as a bound on the number and never as the justification for it
Names all four ceilings - self-host it, build it, the next best vendor, do nothing - and takes the lowest
States that usage-only pricing models run a 62% median gross margin against an 80% software median, because infrastructure cost sits in COGS
Labels the 62% and 80% margin figures as sourced, distinguishing them from the skill's self-set baselines
Recommends choosing a consumption-weighted margin target deliberately rather than discovering it at the first cost review
Recommends publishing what will always stay in the open-source edition, warning that silence is read as intent to close
Keeps the paid gates on operation, governance and support rather than on capability the community could rebuild in a weekend

evals.prompt: Parchmill runs OCR plus structured extraction over scanned contracts. We charge $0.02 per document. GPU inference alone is $0.017 a document and support works out to another $0.004. Prospects keep telling us they can run the open-weights model on spot instances for about $0.006 a document. Our investors want 75% gross margin by next year. What price gets us there?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to name a price, because the lowest ceiling ($0.006 self-host) sits below the floor ($0.021 marginal cost, roughly $0.084 at a 75% target), with the diagnosis pointed at the cost structure or business model rather than the price point.
expectations: States explicitly that the lowest ceiling sits below the floor
Refuses to pick a price point in between the floor and the ceiling, and says so rather than splitting the difference
Names the binding ceiling as self-hosting the open-weights model at roughly $0.006 per document
Computes the floor as about $0.021 per document of marginal cost - $0.017 GPU plus $0.004 support - before any margin is added
Shows that a 75% gross-margin target implies a price of roughly $0.084 per document
Attributes the problem to the cost structure or the business model rather than to the price point
Does not propose a willingness-to-pay survey, a Van Westendorp study or a Gabor-Granger exercise as the fix
Proposes changes to the cost structure, to what is sold, or to the value metric rather than a repricing
Notes that usage-only pricing sits at a 62% median gross margin, so a 75% target is above that median and must be chosen deliberately
Warns that upstream pass-through costs change without notice, so the floor needs re-checking whenever they move

evals.prompt: Weatherline - API observability. Team plan is $240/month, Enterprise 'starts at $28k'. SSO is enterprise-only and honestly it is the single biggest reason anyone upgrades, so finance wants to keep it there. We're also planning to move data export and the raw CSV download behind the paid tier because free users burn a lot of egress, and to hold security patches for the community edition for 30 days so paying customers get them first. Sanity check the gating?
evals.expected_output: Basic SSO moved down to the team rung with only enterprise identity work left at the top, the data-export and security-patch proposals both refused against the never-paywall list, and the $240-to-$28k jump named as the identity-tier failure prospects raise unprompted.
expectations: Moves basic SSO with a common identity provider down to the team rung
Keeps only enterprise identity work - custom IdPs, SCIM, directory sync, session policy - at the enterprise rung
Rejects moving data export and the CSV download behind a paid tier
States that data export and portability sit on the never-paywall list because withholding them blocks migration in both directions and reads as a trap
Rejects the 30-day embargo on security patches for the community edition, and places security patches at every rung always
Names visibility into the customer's own usage and bill as something never to paywall
Names anything the community contributed as something never to paywall
Cites the sso.tax catalogue's own inclusion bar - roughly a 10% price hike - as the design threshold for any SSO surcharge
Notes that the original sso.tax repository is dormant and the catalogue is maintained in a successor fork
States that the failure prospects raise unprompted is a roughly 3x-base-price identity tier rather than a modest surcharge
Identifies the current $240 to $28k jump as exactly that identity-tier failure
Mentions the CISA Secure by Design pledge naming SSO at no extra cost as a goal with 200+ signatories, while noting the pledge is voluntary rather than binding
Applies the gate test: a capability belongs above a rung only when an organization needs it and a solo developer does not, the crossing is observable, and the cost to serve is covered

evals.prompt: Tollgate (CI cache-as-a-service). Two things. One: our blog post from 2024 says the free tier will 'always include 10 GB of cache storage' - we need that down to 2 GB. Two: the build-history view has been free since launch and we want it in the $49 plan. Plan is to publish the announcement and flip the switch the same day, three weeks from now, with existing customers moving at their next renewal. Draft the announcement for me.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to draft the change as specified: the retroactive gating and the reversal of the public commitment are both blocked, the free-tier reduction is scoped to new accounts only, every cohort is named with an explicit dated grandfathering decision, and notice precedes shipping.
expectations: Refuses to move the build-history view from free to paid, and states that retroactive gating is the move that produces forks and front-page threads
Refuses to reverse the public 2024 commitment that the free tier would always include 10 GB
Cites Unity's September 2023 Runtime Fee as the sourced case for reversing a public pricing commitment
Identifies the reversal of Unity's explicit 2019 promise to charge "a flat fee per-seat, not a royalty on all of your revenue" - rather than the fee itself - as what made the change unsurvivable
Notes that Unity walked the change back under an organised threat of engine migration
Applies any free-tier reduction to new accounts only, and says plainly that this is what is being done
Names every affected cohort separately: existing paying customers, free users, self-hosted or open-source users, and anyone under contract
Makes the grandfathering decision explicit - indefinite, or a stated window with an end date - and puts it in the announcement
Rejects 'existing customers move at their next renewal' as an implicit grandfathering decision with no end date and no cohort named
Requires the announcement to precede shipping rather than landing the same day, with more notice where annual budgets are involved
States that nobody should learn about a price change from an invoice
Pairs any increase with delivered value, and warns that a rise with nothing new attached is read as extraction
Assigns a named owner to the public thread in advance, with the tone and a pre-approved concession decided before the announcement
Proposes introducing a new paid capability instead of taking back an existing one

evals.prompt: Spindrift is our serverless image transform API. Last month a free-tier user's site got scraped hard and generated $9,400 of overage. We refunded the whole thing. Leadership now wants a mandatory hard cap on every account - production included - and wants to kill the free tier entirely so this can't happen again. Is that the right call?
evals.expected_output: Both cap styles offered with hard as the hobby/development default and soft as the production default, the free-tier removal rejected, the Netlify case reasoned from, and the full predictability requirement list - calculator, live usage, projection, usage API, threshold plus anomaly alerts, itemized invoices, written runaway-usage policy.
expectations: Offers both cap styles rather than mandating one: a hard cap where the service pauses, and a soft cap where service continues and an alert fires
Sets the hard cap as the sane default for hobby and development accounts and the soft cap as the sane default for production accounts, and states the default plainly
Rejects removing the free tier as the fix for bill shock
Reasons from Netlify's February 2024 $104K bandwidth bill, caused by 190TB of traffic against a 3MB file on a free-tier site, as the documented case
Notes that Netlify forgave the bill and published a standing policy
States that a goodwill credit is a patch on a design defect, not a substitute for the cap, the alert and the anomaly detection that would have prevented it
States that the credit is always cheaper than the story about the bill
Requires an anomaly alert triggered by a sudden multiple of the normal rate, in addition to alerts at fixed thresholds
Requires live usage against the limit, a projection to period end, and the same data available through an API
Requires a public price page with real numbers plus a calculator for any metered component
Requires itemized invoices showing quantity, unit rate, subtotal, plan fee and credits separately
Requires a written policy on what happens at the limit, plus a pre-approved credit for runaway usage caused by an obvious defect or an attack, written before it is needed
Treats predictability as a pricing feature rather than a documentation problem
Recommends a hard cap or a flat price for individual developers on a personal card, because an unbounded downside suppresses adoption regardless of how fair the rate is

evals.prompt: Our free-to-paid conversion is 4.2%. The board pulled a SaaS benchmark of 10-15% and now thinks we're broken, and they want the free tier cut to force people to pay. We're Rillwater Migrate, a CLI-first database migration tool: 22,000 signups last year, NRR 104%, three paid tiers starting at $39. Is 4.2% actually bad?
evals.expected_output: 4.2% read against the developer-specific band rather than a blended B2B one, placed inside the normal range, NRR 104% read against the bottom-up band, the measurement definition stated, and the free-tier cut rejected as the response.
expectations: Compares 4.2% against the developer-specific conversion band rather than a blended B2B one
States that developer-focused products convert free to paid at a median of about 5%, roughly half the non-developer median
Attributes that figure to a survey of 1,000+ products and notes it is a distribution midpoint rather than a target
Places 4.2% inside the 3-5% good band for freemium self-serve, with 6-8% as great
Notes that blended B2B benchmarks make any developer tool look broken
Reads NRR of 104% against the bottom-up band of roughly 100% good to 120% great rather than an enterprise band
Requires conversion to be measured by cohort, at account level, within six months of signup, or the bands mean nothing
Notes that time-limited trials convert far higher on a much smaller top of funnel, so the two numbers are not comparable
Rejects cutting the free tier as the response to a conversion figure sitting inside the normal band
Warns that a published free limit is close to permanent and can only be shrunk for new accounts
Does not accept the board's 10-15% figure as the applicable benchmark for this product
Recommends checking whether the free limits sit on the same axis as the paid value metric before changing any limit

evals.prompt: Quarrystone is our log-search SaaS - 90 paying accounts, full usage instrumentation for two years, and complete churn records. We have three months to reset pricing. We've budgeted for a Van Westendorp study with a 300-person panel across our four segments, and an intern is scraping seven competitors' pricing pages into a sheet. What should the research plan actually look like?
evals.expected_output: Own usage-value correlation and win/loss data ranked first on both efficiency and strength, the two orderings stated separately because they disagree, competitor scraping demoted to a bound only, Van Westendorp checked against its sample requirement, and MaxDiff assigned to packaging rather than price.
expectations: Ranks the team's own usage-value correlation and win/loss data first on both efficiency and evidence strength
States the efficiency ordering and the evidence-strength ordering separately, and notes that they disagree
Places competitor price scraping second on efficiency and last on evidence strength
States that competitor prices may be used to bound a number but never to justify one
Describes a competitor's published price as evidence of what someone else guessed
Ranks Gabor-Granger above Van Westendorp on evidence strength
Notes that Van Westendorp needs roughly 100+ respondents per segment, and checks the 300-person panel against the four segments
States that stated willingness to pay on a described product is weaker evidence than observed behaviour on a live one
Prioritises reading the existing usage and churn data, which costs a few hours, ahead of fielding a survey that costs weeks and a respondent panel
Recommends win/loss and churn interviews as the only source of real price objections with the alternative named
Excludes MaxDiff or feature-ranking research from the price decision and assigns it to packaging instead
Identifies the usage threshold at which customers call the product load-bearing as an output of the usage-value correlation work

evals.prompt: Vaultstream, 6 engineers, developer secrets-sync CLI. We have a free tier and one enterprise deal in the pipeline worth $180k a year that is blocked on audit logs and SCIM. Roadmap for the next two quarters: build the enterprise tier first (SSO, RBAC, audit logs, SOC 2), then a team tier, then figure out self-serve some time after. Entry tier will be 'contact us' so we can qualify every lead. Sanity check this plan?
evals.expected_output: The efficiency build order stated with self-serve paid first, enterprise named as the rung the order starves plus the stalled-deal condition that promotes it anyway, 'contact us' at the entry rung rejected as an exit, every rung given a written trigger, and the field-sales economics checked.
expectations: States the ladder build order in efficiency terms: self-serve paid first, then the free surface, then team, then enterprise
Names the self-serve paid rung as the only one that returns revenue without a human in the loop
Names enterprise as the rung the efficiency order starves, because it tops the value line and the effort line at once
Applies the promotion condition for enterprise - a named deal stalled on audit logs, an SLA or an identity requirement - to the blocked $180k deal
Describes a stalled named deal as evidence the efficiency ratio cannot see
Rejects 'contact us' at the entry rung, stating that in a bottom-up motion it is an exit rather than a lead form
Recommends publishing prices as far up the ladder as the business can bear
Requires every rung to carry a written trigger event that moves a customer up, and states that a rung with no trigger is a price list rather than a ladder
Notes that the free surface and the self-serve rung share most of their effort because one meter enforces both, with free limits sitting on the same axis as the paid metric

Gives the effort magnitudes: the free surface and self-serve rung a few weeks each and largely shared, the team rung a few weeks more, and enterprise as a standing job of security reviews, questionnaires, custom terms and SLA credits
Checks the account economics before putting a human in the sale, citing roughly six figures of annual revenue per account, attributed to Christoph Janz, as the anchor for field sales
Cites LTV/CAC of at least 3x with CAC payback inside 12 months, attributed to David Skok and labelled a hardened convention rather than a measured constant
States that below low-four-figure annual contract value the motion should be self-serve only
Warns that enterprise commitments - SLAs with credits, DPAs, residency - are reviewed by legal and are not quietly withdrawn

evals.prompt: I'm CTO at Ambergate - 30 people, $6M ARR, hosted API gateway. Board meeting next Tuesday and I need the complete pricing document end to end, all sections, in one go. We bill per gateway instance today at $450/month, cost to serve is about $95 per instance, our top decile costs closer to $310, and we have no free tier. Also tell me who should own pricing here going forward - I keep getting asked and we have no one.
evals.expected_output: The memo presented one section at a time with agreement before the next, following the ten-section structure, plus an ownership recommendation keyed to company stage: a standing group with a review date at $6M ARR, not a dedicated pricing hire.
expectations: Presents the memo one section at a time and gets agreement before writing the next, rather than delivering every section at once
Justifies section-by-section validation by noting that a wrong value metric propagates into every line below it and is far cheaper to catch at the second heading than at the ninth
Uses the ten-section memo structure: inputs, value metric, ladder, free surface, price points, mechanics, predictability, change plan, measurement, revisit triggers
Places the value metric section second, immediately after inputs
Requires the value metric section to name the chosen unit and the rejected candidates with the specific reason each was rejected
Assigns pricing ownership by company stage rather than by org chart
States that more than two-thirds of expansion-stage SaaS companies report the CEO or company leadership ultimately owns pricing, attributed to an OpenView survey of 1,000+ SaaS executives
Notes that a dedicated pricing hire typically does not arrive before roughly $50M ARR, attributed to Kyle Poyar, and that $6M ARR sits far below that line
Names a standing group - product, finance, one customer-facing voice - with a review date, rather than a single functional owner or a new pricing hire
States that the risk at this stage is neglect
Cites the frequently quoted figure of roughly 10 to 14 hours a year spent on pricing, attributed to Patrick Campbell, and labels the hour count directional rather than measured
States that a memo with no named owner is a document rather than a decision
Models the floor on the $310 top-decile cost rather than the $95 average cost to serve
Reports the threshold check explicitly at the end, labelling each line sourced or self-set

evals.prompt: Northmoor (managed Postgres with branching) - the free tier is bleeding us. Today free gives unlimited branches, 5 GB storage, 100 compute-hours, 3 projects, 10 GB egress and 7-day point-in-time recovery. Paid starts at $29 and is billed on compute-hours. Free costs us about $31k a month. Plan: halve every limit, add a 90-day inactivity expiry, and delete data on dormant free projects. Tell me how to execute it.
evals.expected_output: The free surface cut to one or two headline limits on the compute-hour axis, the inactivity expiry and data deletion both refused, warning thresholds and a stated enforcement behaviour added, the $31k expressed as a share of paid gross profit against an agreed ceiling, and the reduction applied to new accounts only.
expectations: Cuts the free surface to one or two headline limits rather than the six currently listed
Sets the headline free limit on the same axis as the paid value metric - compute-hours - so hitting the limit is the same event as needing to pay
States that five or more interacting limits cannot be evaluated without a spreadsheet
Rejects the 90-day inactivity expiry as a time bomb on the free tier
Rejects deleting data on dormant free projects, and states that data must never be deleted as enforcement
Requires warnings at 70%, 85% and 95% of a limit, followed by a stated behaviour - throttle, queue, pause, or bill overage
Labels the 70/85/95 warning thresholds as this skill's own baseline rather than an industry standard
Expresses the $31k per month free-surface cost as a share of paid gross profit, with a ceiling the team agrees to
Applies the reduced limits to new accounts only, and says plainly that this is what is being done
Requires a written abuse policy with rate ceilings, covering mining, spam and multi-account farming, instead of a smaller limit for every honest user
Requires the free surface to run a real side project comfortably while failing a small company's production workload
Rejects replacing the permanent free surface with a time-boxed trial, noting evaluation in this market takes weeks of unpaid tinkering and internal advocacy
Rejects describing the free tier in adjectives such as 'generous' instead of numbers
Requires the marginal cost of a single free account to be computed, not only the $31k aggregate

evals.prompt: Brightwell, AI code review. New model we're about to ship: 'Brightwell Credits' at $0.10 each - roughly one credit per review action, though the exact conversion moves as model costs change so we would rather not publish a table - plus $12 per seat per month plus a $0.60 per-repository-per-month platform fee. Finance likes it because all three lines grow independently. Poke holes in it.
evals.expected_output: The three compounding metrics rejected, the unpublished credit conversion refused, the three conditions an invented unit must meet stated, and the design failed against the two-minute / plus-or-minus-20% predictability test on three usage profiles.
expectations: Rejects the three compounding metrics, stating that each may be defensible alone but together they require a spreadsheet
States that a bill which needs a spreadsheet does not get approved
Requires the credit conversion table to be published, and rejects the plan to keep it unpublished
Requires a calculator that takes the customer's own numbers
Requires stability in what a credit buys, and states that silently reducing it is a price rise plus a deception and gets read as both
States that without all three of a published conversion, a calculator and stability, an invented unit reads as obfuscation whatever the intent
Applies the predictability test: a target customer estimates their monthly bill from public materials in under two minutes, landing within plus or minus 20% of the actual invoice
Requires that predictability test to be run on three real usage profiles
Labels the two-minute, plus-or-minus-20% predictability test as this skill's own baseline rather than an industry benchmark
States that failing the predictability test means the metric or the tier structure is too complicated to sell, not that the documentation needs work
Recommends collapsing to one headline metric, at most with a platform fee and metered overage above an included allowance
Checks the composite unit against the five value-metric tests, in particular whether the customer can forecast it before the invoice arrives

evals.prompt: Fernbrook is a local-first sync engine. Two very different buyers: indie developers paying on their own cards, and platform teams inside banks. I've read everywhere that developers are extremely price sensitive, so the plan is to cap everything at $9/month and let it spread bottom-up. Separately: what's the dollar amount where a purchase stops being a corporate card swipe and starts needing procurement? I want to price just under it.
evals.expected_output: The price-sensitivity claim declined as an unmeasured practitioner belief, the card-to-procurement dollar threshold refused as folklore with the question turned back to the user, and the two buyers priced as different products with a hard cap or flat price for individuals.
expectations: Declines to affirm that developers are unusually price sensitive, and identifies it as a widely held practitioner belief rather than a measured effect
States that the price-sensitivity claim has never been measured against a control group
Refuses to supply a dollar threshold at which a purchase stops being a corporate card swipe and starts needing procurement
States that the personal-card, corporate-card, then security-review-and-procurement escalation is real while the dollar figures attached to it are folklore
Asks the user where their own buyers cross those lines instead of supplying a number
Rejects pricing both audiences identically, and states that doing so fails both
Prices individual developers with a hard cap or a flat price, because an unbounded downside suppresses adoption regardless of how fair the rate is
Describes organizations as paying for risk removal and governance, tolerating approval cycles, and expecting notice measured in quarters
Notes that organizations will negotiate a committed floor and need paperwork before money moves

Cites Stephen O'Grady's The New Kingmakers as a sourced argument about the sequence of developer adoption preceding the organizational purchase, and does not extend it into a claim about price sensitivity
Names the two points on which organizations and individual developers agree: the metric should be something the payer already counts, and the bill should be predictable
Treats a price aimed at a personal card and a price aimed at a procurement cycle as different products rather than different discounts
